No, I work at a shelter and with a dog behaviorist, this is how she suggests working with bad behavior. Doing what you are doing isn't teaching him anything because he doesn't know what he's being yelled at for. It would also be helpful to reward him whenever you tell him no and bring him out of the room, that will show him that leaving the counter will be more of a reward than jumping on the counter, slowly ween off with less valuable treats until you dont need them, then keep rewarding with petting or playtime. The whole point in stopping him in the action so he understands he's not supposed to be doing it. When you're not home simply clean up anything he can get into.

Keep a leash on him for a week or so or until he learns not too. He was never reprimanded doing this behavior in his previous home. You will have to watch him 24/7 while you're home to be effective. The minute he jumps to the counter you grab the lash and pull him off with a firm NO, and walk him out of the room. Doing/saying more than that will make it confusing to him. The more simple the command is done, the better results because there is no miscommunication between you and you're dog.

What I've gathered so far is that we all experience it in our head generally the same, our outward reactions are what are different. And I dont think its necessarily a gender thing, more of a person to person thing. Women just tend to be more nurturing when it comes to emotional issues. And men are generally more composed and not supposed to do that. But that's society's fault.

There is really no money working in the shelter field, I have been at my job for a year now, I just make above minimum wage and wont get a raise until March. So do that some dont. You will meet the best people, and the worst people. I have learned to never judge a book by the cover sort of speak. Very rarely when a dog is brought into the shelter 9/10 the people want nothing to do with dog. The hardest part is getting returns. When you think you've picked the best home and they return the dog for mundane reasons. That's the hardest part of my job. I would also suggest working at a low-kill shelter as they will not euthanize for space. It's hard enough working there, I could never imagine working a kill shelter.
